This knowledge update will delve into applying machine learning algorithms to predict the following material properties: diffusion coefficients, phase transformations, and mechanical properties; showcase a new dimension of microscopy sample extraction for predicting material behavior; and explore recent advancements using physics-informed neural networks.

To analyze the decay $T_{cc}^{	au +} \to D^{	au} D D^{	au} \to D^{	au} D^{*	au} D$ and investigate potential contributions from other hadronic decay channels, we employ an approach that takes into account the interplay between $D^{	au} D$ and $D^{	au} 	au$ final state interactions. Our calculation shows that the former effect surpasses the latter by at least 8 times and suggests that the full hadronic width of $T_{cc}^{	au +}$ could be lower than the estimate of 1 keV for the semi-leptonic width.

The development of complex large-scale systems, including smart buildings and their energy consumption patterns, necessitates a deeper understanding of their underlying dynamics. Current research in machine learning and data-driven methods has shown potential in uncovering this complexity by identifying relevant factors and their interactions. Nevertheless, there's a lack of consensus on the most effective approach or feature representation. In this study, we've found that graph neural networks are ideally suited for building-scale data analysis and subspace learning. We've established that these networks can be effectively reduced in size while maintaining their performance in identifying relevant features. Using real-world building data from the PDC dataset, we've demonstrated the efficacy of GNNs in discovering meaningful patterns and identifying limiting factors in building energy efficiency.

In a 1986 paper, Sidon sets within the finite affine plane were defined and the comprehensive problem of identifying all possible Sidon sets was posed. Recent research, building on work by Paul Erdos, has made progress on this problem by proving certain inequalities related to the size and number of Sidon sets. These inequalities, derived using a complex series of arguments, have ultimately allowed for the identification and confirmation of all possible Sidon sets in a specific sub-case. Notably, this confirmation employs a novel use of hyperbolas and ellipses to represent certain patterns in the plane.

Choosing efficient sampling methods is vital in various disciplines such as computer science, physics, and biology. Previous studies mainly focused on finding the most efficient unsampled elements and random sampling approaches were rarely tested. This work compares the efficiency of random and non-random sampling of binary matrices. Our results show that the latter can be significantly more efficient, especially when the probability distribution is not uniform, by as much as four times faster in certain cases. We also introduce new sampling algorithms based on the dynamic tree data structure, providing higher throughput and lower overhead than existing methods. These improvements result in substantial speed increases, from a 1.04 to 14.01 times faster than the rapid spanners-based method, depending on the matrix type. We demonstrate that selecting smallest parents in the dynamic tree is both a compact representation of a binary matrix and an efficient means of sampling unscaled elements. Our work focuses on binary matrices, but we outline a more general process for scaling parent selections and demonstrate its effectiveness on different types of graphs.

A unified approach to solving the DGLAP equations and fitting parton distribution functions at varying scales is presented. The method utilizes an iterative process that applies the DGLAP equations in conjunction with a technique for matching PDFs across different scales. The process is an extension of the Renorm Group Evolution technique, initially developed for evolving PDFs at a single scale, and is demonstrated to be equivalent to solving the DGLAP equations with certain constraints. However, when fitting PDFs at multiple scales, the method is differentiated from standard DGLAP fitting techniques, as it applies the DGLAP equations in an iterative manner. This procedure is shown to be a special case of the multi-scale Renorm Group Evolution technique and is demonstrated to be DGLAP-compatible. The method is further validated by being reducible to standard fitting techniques at each stage of evolution, and is shown to be a reliable and accurate technique for determining PDFs at various scales. The technique is successfully applied to fit the NNPDF31 PDF sets and determines PDFs at different scales with high accuracy. Furthermore, the growth of the discrepancy between PDFs at different scales, as one evolves further, is quantified and demonstrated to be a reliable measure of the uncertainty in PDFs.

This document outlines the concepts and results obtained from using the ELKI data mining framework in high-performance computing.  Our goal in using the Java-based Elki framework was to assess its capabilities in solving data mining tasks, such as clustering, density-based and supervised learning, on supercomputing systems. Our research focused on evaluating how the architecture of Intel's Ascension node affects performance by comparing distributed and sequential data mining operations. These experiments were repeated for both local and remote data processing scenarios. Our analysis revealed that the Elki framework significantly boosts performance and scalability through efficient data distribution and parallel computation. Consequently, achieving up to 500 core-hours of computing power with 512 cores, a feat previously inaccessible with traditional data mining software. Our study conclusively demonstrates the enduring value of the Elki framework in high-performance computing applications.

We present a novel technique for generating robust, stable, and tunable microcombs with high spectral resolution. By combining the capabilities of a microcomb and a fiber Mach-Zehnder interferometer with parallel and anti-parallel pump-sidebands, we demonstrate the creation of distinct, isolated frequency lines within the microcomb spectrum. These lines can be dynamically adjusted by varying the difference between the interferometer's optical paths, thereby enabling precise control over the microcomb's frequency. This protocol can be widely utilized for advanced spectroscopy, tunable filter applications, and precision frequency metrology.

We establish that the arithmetic transformation semigroup corresponding to the additive group of integers is characterized by a distinctive invariant subgroup that exhibits certain mixing and faithfulness properties. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the decay rate of correlations in this semigroup is governed by a non-degenerate polynomial with a leading coefficient of 1, but we present evidence suggesting that the upper bound defined by a specific constant is indeed the optimal choice.

Researchers use quasi neural networks to study the large-scale behavior of deep neural networks, specifically those trained with momentum. However, the factor that influences these networks the most is their architecture. To overcome this limitation, a study focuses on a specific class of networks, which it claims can accurately represent the training and data-driven dynamics of both stationary and non-stationary environments with high precision. Moreover, the study reveals that the neural tangent kernel associated with these networks has an exponentially decaying eigenvalue spectrum, a result that is independent of the network's size. To confirm these findings, the study presents numerical evidence supporting the theory.

In contrast to a long-standing assumption within holographic theory, we demonstrate that monogamy of mutual information - a principle linking distinct subsystems - cannot be applied to bulk regions without incorporating unusual, non-causal dependencies. Consequently, in theories with monogamy of mutual information, boundary entropies in thermodynamic equilibrium must inevitably sum to a value greater than the boundary entropy of a single, entirety system. In order to maintain consistency with causality, theories in which mutual information is monogamous must be restricted to those with no more than a single, single-sided Rindler region - effectively reducing them to theories akin to the CKMW model. We further verify that, in order to avoid an entropy excess exceeding the area law, boundaries in these theories must possess a level of entropy per degree of freedom at least double that predicted by the Cardy-Calabrese formula.

In this paper, local state probabilities of specific lattice models are calculated 
expressed in irreducible characters of symmetric groups, with a further demonstration 
that an integral representation of these probabilities is possible in cases where 
branching rules apply. Examples are provided to illustrate the efficacy of this 
integral representation, with particular examination of a related model involving 
alternating group symmetry.

This research investigates how to integrate the capabilities of various stabilization methods, all of which are rooted in randomized Kaczmarz (RK) algorithm variants. These techniques are utilized to enhance convergence in online learning settings where data arrival is sequential. Given that each stabilization method modifies the RK algorithm in a distinct way, directly combining them would require individual analyses, which can be complex. To avoid this computational intensity, our approach develops a unified framework to combine stabilization methods. By converting each stabilization method into an additional term in an iterative process, we create a combined algorithm with all stabilization methods combined. Through our conceptual model, any stabilization method for the RK algorithm can be combined with others, resulting in novel algorithms with enhanced stability and robustness. Furthermore, our theoretical analysis proves that the combined algorithms share the same average iteration complexity with their individual stabilization method counterparts. Additionally, our experiments validate theoretical findings and showcase the practical benefits of combining stabilization methods, highlighting the importance of data quality on algorithm performance.

The application of non-linear co-addition algorithms such as median or clipped-mean values disrupts the signal from point sources and star shapes, aside from maintaining the desired signal output. In contrast to linear combinations, these algorithms inherently alter the point source profile and thus induce artifacts. To rectify this issue, we have developed algorithms that restore a consistent and unaltered PSF for any co-added image, utilizing a reference PSF and our new algorithms can be used to create PSF catalogues prior to data release, allowing the removal of stellar shapes and signal from unknown objects even after multiple co-added iterations. We have provided detailed instruction on how to utilize these algorithms and have made the necessary code and tests publicly available.

We provide a precise and rigorous analysis of the chordal SLE process, specifically its imaginary components, using a novel approach based on conformal maps associated with stochastic Loewner evolution (SLE). This involves developing the imaginary components of SLE into a more general framework called the imaginary surface evolution (ISE), a new family of stochastic processes governing the growth of "imaginary surfaces" in the complex plane. Our work establishes a one-to-one correspondence between ISE and SLE, enabling the derivation of key scaling and symmetry properties for SLE from its imaginary components. Additionally, our study offers a unique and intuitive understanding of the SLE process as encircling the origin of the complex plane with "imaginary surfaces," providing a more transparent connection between SLE and its tree-related representations, specifically the tree-valued Evans-Shephard martingale.

Using an explicit time-integration method for the Navier-Stokes equations, we obtain a precise bound on the norm of the velocity's derivatives. This results in a condition that implies the decay of rough norms, leading to the observation that small disturbances can result in large velocity gradients over long periods of time. This finding aligns with real-world experiments involving chaotic fluid flows, which exhibit rough velocity profiles. We demonstrate that our analysis is consistent with rough perturbation theory's predictions from [A. Chorin, 2021].

This research introduces an enhanced QQC verification protocol, CVQC, designed to execute quantum circuit measurements without requiring a quantum computer. CVQC improves upon previous research by incorporating advanced quantum algorithms and neural networks, enabling verification on a much broader range of circuits, including complicated ones, at significantly accelerated speeds, from hundreds to millions of times faster. Additionally, the CVQC protocol boasts heightened assurance levels for its results, achieved through the integration of multiple validation processes, including cross-validation and redundant calculations, thus providing both reliable and efficient circuit verification. A publicly accessible, user-friendly interface has been created for easy deployment, along with regular updates to incorporate the latest advancements in artificial intelligence and machine learning, empowering the global research community to continually enhance the protocol.

The development of cell-based research holds significant potential for discovering novel treatments and understanding cellular biology. Cell membranes serve as a boundary between cells and their surroundings, and accurate representation of cell geometry is critical for biomedical analysis, particularly in segmentation and tracking tasks. However, existing methods fall short in capturing the intricate geometry of membranes in microscopic images. To address this limitation, we introduce MemGen, a novel deep generative model capable of generating highly detailed membrane syntheses. By synthesizing a vast number of cell membranes, MemGen creates a rich population of synthetic cells, and trains a conditional Variational Autoencoder (cVAE) using these synthetic cells. The model is conditioned on rich semantic cell attributes, allowing for the generation of cells with diverse semantic properties. Through analysis, we demonstrate MemGen's effectiveness in improving biological image segmentation by downscaling the total memory requirement of the model. Additionally, we showcase MemGen's capability to handle absent or missing regions in cell membranes by using a memory augmentation technique. By releasing MemGen publicly, we aim to facilitate advancements in cell shape analysis and promote further innovation in the field.

Reinforcement learning persists in the mind of the public due to its potential to solve problems autonomously, but its application in geometric tasks reveals a crucial limitation - the persistence of features. This has been validated by multiple studies, which have consistently found that beyond a certain point in training, the progress made by reinforcement learning algorithms stagnates. This phenomenon has significant implications across multiple domains, including biology, psychology, and artificial intelligence. Previous research attempted to explain this feature persistence, but their findings were either partially supportive or introduced new concepts to account for the effect. Moreover, no studies have successfully eliminated the persistence of features in geometric tasks. This has raised questions about whether persistence is an inevitable result of reinforcement learning or if it is simply a sign of an algorithm that has reached its limits. This study aims to address these questions by presenting a novel method that substantially mitigates feature persistence and improves the performance of reinforcement learning algorithms. This approach differs from previous research by incorporating temporal logic instead of utilizing a straightforward reward structure. Temporal logic offers a more effective way to direct attention and eliminate distracting features, as it allows for the formulation of logic laws that cover specific sequences of events. Our study showcases the potential of this new method by applying it to a series of complex tasks, which demonstrates its capability to significantly reduce feature persistence and improve the performance of reinforcement learning algorithms.

To resolve the challenge of freezing in three-dimensional dipolar models, a new algorithm called Newtonian ECMC (NECMC) has been devised. NECMC builds upon an earlier method known as ECMC, by incorporating a Newtonian iteration to address the stiff equations involved in simulating dipolar interactions. This variant successfully prevents artificial freezing at low temperatures in the simulations, while maintaining the ECMC algorithm's ability to explore the system's equilibrium properties. NECMC is then applied to a number of 3D dipolar systems, ranging from simple collections of particles to more complex structures, in order to study their collective behavior and crystal formation.

Data augmentation plays a crucial role in enhancing the performance of deep learning-based sound event detection models, but its optimal application remains unclear. A particular challenge lies in the diverse nature of sound datasets, which renders many traditional aggregation techniques ineffective. A few methods have been used in sound processing, but their effectiveness has not been thoroughly evaluated across various sound event classification datasets. This study aims to address this knowledge gap by systematically examining eight data augmentation techniques in conjunction with three aggregation methods on two widely used sound datasets. The impact of different aggregation methods on three deep neural network architectures was investigated, while also considering the influence of different model inputs, dataset characteristics, and replication. Our analysis reveals that certain data augmentation techniques complement specific aggregation methods, ultimately yielding improved classification performance. Specifically, we found that utility Currying and SpecAugment yielded top results on the DCASE 2016 and 2019 benchmark challenges.

The theory of signal representation utilizes a superposition property to guarantee complete recovery of a signal encoded through a non-unique combination of vectors. Various networks, such as those utilizing non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) or federated learning systems, rely on superposition principles. A key factor in ensuring this theory's applicability is that the dictionaries should not be singular. This raises the question: can bounded invertibility be used as an alternative criterion to ensure reliable signal reconstruction. This question is crucial given the numerous applications where superposition is inherent but dictionaries are not necessarily unique (such as NOMA or federated learning systems). We examine this problem, providing numerical examples that demonstrate how the bounded invertibility of dictionaries offers a viable signal reconstruction solution. Additionally, we explore the connection between the condition number of dictionaries and the required number of iterations for reliable reconstruction. This study offers a practical method to guarantee reliable reconstruction in systems relying on the superposition property with bounded invertibility.

This study introduces an iterative method to generate spectrogram-based maps that closely resemble the Spectrogram Level Set Estimation (SLSE) algorithm. By extending SLSE, we propose Spectrogram Level Set Detection (SLSD), a new approach that uses a point-wise comparison heuristic or a constant bandwidth strategy for spectral analysis. Our developed SLSD method surpasses existing techniques in terms of accuracy, offering a more precise and closer approximation to level sets. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical connection between our iterative SLSD algorithm and the continuous time gradient descent method. Our results demonstrate that Spectrogram Level Set Detection achieves superior performance over other techniques in a range of test cases.

We suggest a method to observe the synchronized behavior of a complex system using time-series data and apply it to a nonlinear dynamical system with a known solution. This approach relies on modifying a time-series dataset to create a space-time map, which is then analyzed through a customized statistical measure to identify the dominant patterns. By applying this method to a system displaying global synchronization and translating it into a stability index, we demonstrate the ability to detect the number of synchronized clusters in a complex system. Furthermore, we illustrate the applicability of our method by evaluating a nonlinear dynamical system in both periodic and chaotic states.

We introduce a novel, versatile module called Physical Movement Module (PHYM) that facilitates realistic simulation of particle motion in space, incorporating various physical factors such as gravity, elasticity, and energy transfer. Built with a component-based architecture, this module is designed to be adaptable to multiple scenarios and can easily be integrated with popular 3D animation software. Furthermore, PHYM's comprehensive interface allows for the subtle manipulation of any physical property, enabling both precise and intuitive control over simulations. A comprehensive demonstration showcases the module's capabilities through a series of practical examples spanning multiple disciplines, including animation, visual effects, and scientific visualization.

The capability of a quantum information engine to operate in continuous and discrete modes is explored. Unlike the standard perspective, where a measurement event halts the quantum system's evolution, our model considers the impact of continuous, real-time measurement data on the underlying dynamics. A mathematical framework, rooted in quantum stochastic calculus, facilitates the study of the quantum information engine's evolution while taking into account the influence of external thermal radiation fields and its subsequently damaged coherence. Our research demonstrates that continuous measurement differs fundamentally from the standard model, leading to a more complex understanding of the engine's performance. Ultimately, we identify key conditions for error-free discrete data transmission and develop methods to mitigate the effects of noise and maintain coherence in the quantum information engine. Our findings provide valuable insights for designing quantum information engines that leverage continuous measurement processes.

In a tightly packed container, jammed disks are arranged in a stable position, with the application of external force required to move them. This concept has been extended to study stacks of disks in a confined space and their behavior as they jam. Research found that the jamming point of these stacks depends on the disk's shape, with thicker disks jamming at a lower applied force than thinner ones. This unique characteristic holds promise for improving the capacity of storage systems, like molecular motors powering the transport of cargo, by allowing a larger variety of disks to be used, leading to a more efficient energy transfer.

Using cutting-edge satellite data, researchers identified two distinct flavors of each El Niño and La Niña by analyzing the southern equatorial Pacific's precipitation patterns. Corresponding analyses of 15 multimodal climate predictions from various centers revealed different flavors of these three-year climate phenomena may impact global precipitation patterns, with potentially high economic and social impacts if predicted accurately. Notably, combinations of El Niño and La Niña can lead to extreme droughts and floods in various regions, affecting agricultural yields and affecting millions of people. If accurately forecasted, distinct flavors of these three-year climate phenomena could enhance predictions of global food security, market trends, and financial fluctuations in commodity markets, thereby saving governments and industries significant money by allowing for earlier preparations.

Our study explores how various processes at the seedy ground level influence the mass distribution of supermassive black holes. It distinctively sets itself apart from conventional black hole mass studies that generally rely on observations of existing galaxies and their central black holes. Instead, we examine how different heavy seed formation mechanisms and light seeding processes impact the mass spectrum of black holes, particularly in the early universe, by employing a Monte Carlo simulation method. This study is significant as it marks the first Monte Carlo simulation to investigate black hole mass spectra across multiple epochs, from the formation of the universe to the present day. Our simulation takes into account how black hole masses evolve over time, influenced by a dynamic gas environment, as well as stellar feedback, mergers, and other processes. We also develop a simplified model to simulate how these factors contribute to the overall mass spectrum of supermassive black holes. When compared to observational data from the ongoing Event Horizon Telescope project and a recent study on supermassive black holes, our simulated mass spectra show promising results. This research lays the groundwork for utilizing black hole mass statistics as a tool for testing cosmological and astrophysical theories and provides a framework for further investigating the link between supermassive black hole growth and galaxy evolution.

On certain two-dimensional non-unitary lattice structures, there is a flat
band-driven correlation effect where the inherent symmetry of the lattice
becomes a significant factor in determining the properties of the system. A
representative example of this type of behavior can be seen in a two-band
model based on a Hubbard lattice, where the emergence of superconductivity and
a specific type of ferromagnetism is linked to specific symmetry properties and
is influenced by the anisotropy of the lattice. Another instance is seen in
a three-band model exhibiting flat bands, where the correlation effect is
linked to a specific symmetry and is responsible for the emergence of
ferromagnetism and superconductivity. Notably, both examples demonstrate that
the correlation effect can be controlled through lattice anisotropy and symmetry
breakdown, which may have implications for the study of unusual correlation
effects in systems with flat bands.

By combining data from 71 PDB structures and 359 SNPs associated with 34 complex traits, our study explores how protein sequences impact the association between genetic variants and phenotypes. We reveal that the influence of protein sequence differs significantly across distinct traits, with some traits being more susceptible to the effects of specific amino acid substitutions, while others are not. This discovery indicates that incorporating protein information can enhance our comprehension of the genetic underpinnings of certain complex traits, but is unlikely to be beneficial for others.

This research aims to expand upon a previous study by B. Lindner and A. Matthews, examining the existence of 2-designs with a prime number of points and a specific type of automorphism group. Additionally, we investigate the existence of 2-designs with a prime number of points that are resolvable into complete sub-designs, while also possessing a certain automorphism group. Our findings demonstrate that such designs either resemble resolvable transitive linear spaces or specifically tailored designs, with the latter consisting of unique, previously uncategorized designs.

Within the framework of the Dirac Hartree-Fock theory, the total number of particles in a confined system is fixed, but their positions are fully randomized, allowing us to examine how uncertainties in particle positions are connected to other uncertainties, such as in momentum space. A specific relationship in the Coulomb correlation is investigated by analyzing the differences between total and kinetic informational entropies computed in various ways, including through the use of a universal functional and a Thomas-Fermi functional. These computations are carried out for a Coulomb correlation in a spherical, freely decoupling scenario, specifically for a hydrogenic impurity in a nanosphere and electrons in a neutral gas of spherical shape, and the results show that entropy measures of this free decoupling phenomenon are insensitive to the model details used, while its magnitude is roughly $10^{-22}$ ergs. Additionally, a connection is established between the Coulomb correlation effects and the entropy increase caused by it, which is found to be roughly one-third of the kinetic entropy resulting from the universal model, and this ratio is found to be independent of the model and the confinement strength.

Our innovative technique for measuring one-dimensional velocity dispersion has been enhanced by utilizing line velocity measurements from the Medium-Resolution Spectographic Sloan Lensing Pilot Project. The velocity dispersion values obtained through this new method are compared to historical data and also used to calculate additional parameters, including the virial radius, mass-to-light ratio, and the intrinsic shape of the wide binary system. The precision of this new technique in determining velocity dispersion is approximately 8% and shows positive correlation with prior measurements. Furthermore, our new method can efficiently calculate multiple system parameters using data from just two epochs, offering valuable advancements in the field of wide binary study.

We introduce a notion of 'ideal representations' that mirrors the structure of multiple proof strategies in multiplicative linear logic. Conversely, we demonstrate that any such representation can be linked back to a corresponding proof structure through a canonical relationship. This provides a mathematical framework for examining the fundamental connections between meaning and form in linear logic, particularly in the context of focused proof theory.

Previous research suggested that certain interconnected financial time series tend to be in a synchronized state, often predicting their synchronization state using complex network dynamics. In this study, a more straightforward approach using deep learning is taken to predict the synchronization state of time series. Our results indicate that deep learning can be up to 96% effective in predicting the synchronization state of time series, even when those sequences are modified and no longer clearly synchronized. Additionally, our analysis shows that synchronized and anti-synchronized time series exhibit distinct patterns, which can be captured by a classifier trained on these sequences. It's noteworthy that the classifier is capable of detecting modified synchronized states with high accuracy, suggesting that the underlying driver of synchronization is still present even if the synchronization state is no longer clear.

The ability to control quantum systems is a core principle in physics and chemistry, and doing so for an entire reactor is a significant goal. Achieving this control is even more difficult in molecules, where it requires manipulating intense electromagnetic fields to overcome chemical energy barriers. However, such an approach faces a challenge in effectively coordinating the reaction pathway with these electromagnetic fields. This problem is linked to the inadequacy of describing molecular dynamics with a single reaction coordinate, particularly when quantum effects play a role. This research explores a solution by focusing on the central idea that quantum oscillations in molecules can be controlled to modulate the intensity of electromagnetic fields they produce, thus influencing their behavior. This idea is within the reach of current experimental capabilities, and our study provides a straightforward, multi-dimensional approach for achieving this control. This approach simplifies the process of finding suitable pathways for chemical reactions by using coherent states, which are vibrational states that are highly excited and correlated. This methodology is successful in manipulating H+H$_{2}$ collisions to optimize their energy transfer to H$_{2}$ using laser fields that are intense but not too broad. This discovery could significantly impact our ability to control energy transfer in molecular reactions, a key goal in chemistry.

Predicting the click-through rate (CTR) is a fundamental challenge in online advertising. Since visual representations play a crucial role in representing ads, researchers have explored using deep learning models to incorporate ad visuals into CTR prediction models. However, these studies have been hindered by issues such as limited computational resources and the absence of large-scale ad visual datasets. Our work overcomes these challenges by introducing the Click is Cool (CIC) challenge, which includes new benchmarks and state-of-the-art models for CTR prediction that utilize ad visuals. Our analysis reveals that visual ID, a critical ad element, significantly enhances the accuracy of CTR prediction models. With support from leading ad platforms, we release our dataset and competitive results to enable further research on this topic, aiming to bridge the gap between visual understanding and CTR prediction.

To accurately represent the realities of real-world processes, procedures must be defined with concurrency levels that reflect actual demands. Therefore, a theoretical framework for business processes with a specified number of active tasks is developed, which incorporates the concepts of flow objects and transition rates. This model optimizes both resource allocation and process execution time by taking into account the number of active tasks and transition probabilities. The approach involves identifying cycle patterns in the process flow and developing strategies for task execution to minimize wait times, which includes distributing tasks across multiple processes and adjusting the order of task executions. A linear programming technique is used to determine how to distribute and schedule tasks within each process and to minimize the total execution time. The approach is demonstrated through an example process and further illustrated with a simulation, which shows how to determine the optimal number of active tasks and transition probabilities to minimize the execution time of each process.

This research presents a statistical model inspired by physics that uses real-time data from AOD maps and incorporates parameters derived from the study of light interactions with matter. The model works by solving the radiative transfer equation in a statistical context, specifically tailored to address the complex dynamics of wildfire-generated AOD. By leveraging computational power, the model leverages high-frequency information in AOD time-series to provide precise estimates, whereas parameter uncertainty is managed through Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling. The statistical approach is validated through numerous simulations and demonstrated to outperform existing machine learning techniques, showcasing improved accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, the research highlights the potential for statistical models to serve as diagnostic tools, offering insights into the underlying physics of AOD propagation.

Privacy preservation in location-based services (LBS) is deemed essential, yet existing methods are insufficient. These methods either maintains the anonymity of individuals but compromises location privacy or prioritizes location privacy at the expense of data utility. In this research, we introduce a novel framework, referred to as Privacy-enhanced LBS framework, addressing the inherent shortcomings. This framework protects individual and location privacy while promoting data utility by preserving key spatial patterns. To achieve this, we leverage information theory and develop methods to measure privacy losses for both unconditional and conditionally dependent data. A localized artificial immunity algorithm is employed to optimize a dual objective function, ensuring both privacy and utility are protected. In experiments using real-world taxicab data, we showcase the effectiveness of our framework in maintaining differential privacy for both single-source and intercompany data. These results illustrate that our method provides satisfactory privacy and utility protection, outperforming existing approaches.

The study of brain connectivity across disparate sites has gained significant interest, driven by the desire to understand how interconnected brain systems work across various environments and subjects. In contrast to individual-based studies, investigating group differences in brain networks from combined datasets poses a challenge, as variability within each group may outweigh the differences between groups. Furthermore, accumulating additional subjects may fail to enhance between-group differentiation. 

To address these concerns, we developed a novel and robust approach using network-level Bayesian classification to identify distinct groups from inter-site brain networks. Our method effectively minimizes unreliable connections by filtering out low-weight edges, thereby enriching the predictive information extracted from brain networks. As a result, fewer subject samples are required to achieve a certain level of accuracy. We tested our approach using inter-site brain scan data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP) dataset. Our results show that our method surpasses traditional robustness techniques in detecting group differences and yields more stable findings across various datasets. Moreover, our approach allows for the exploration of multiple network-level features and provides subject-level diagnostic capabilities. Given its general applicability, our method can be employed to analyze inter-site brain networks across various disciplines. The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/ashinoshem/RBC_NBC.

We have developed a novel heat fourier integral transform, known as the heat fourier integral, based on the heat equation. This heat fourier integral can be utilized as an alternative to the traditional Fourier transform in function space estimates. Our work includes deriving frequency representation for the heat fourier integral and associated inverse via explicit formulas. Moreover, we have derived concentration of measure inequalities for functions, as well as stochastic processes, via the heat fourier integral. The inverse heat fourier transform has various applications, including the estimation, retrieval, and reconstruction of functions, as well as the second moment analysis of the heat fourier transform of functions. In particular, we have achieved the second moment analysis for functions within $L^p(\mathbb{R})$ or $C^r(\mathbb{R})$ using the heat fourier integral.

Recent advancements in pre-trained language models have significantly improved the performance of monolingual language models, but their applicability to code-mixed text is limited due to issues like missing bilingual context and excessive noise. To bridge this gap, our innovative approach, named SMDBERT, addresses two critical problems in processing code-mixed language. Firstly, we utilize positionally informed multi-encoder learning, incorporating both monolingual and code-mixed pre-trained language models to leverage bilingual context. Secondly, we employ cross-lingual attention techniques, allowing the model to focus on relevant language details, even in the absence of sufficient information. Our results demonstrate substantial enhancements over baseline models in various natural language processing tasks and datasets.

Researchers used first-principles calculations to determine the isotopic effect in H$_{3}$S, a hydrogen sulfide compound that exhibits potential superconducting properties at high pressures. Under pressure, H$_{3}$S changes into a tetragonal structure, in which hydrogen atoms are arranged in a specific pattern, and its electronic properties show a strong similarity to that of solid hydrogen. Our study focused on how the mass of hydrogen isotopes affects the electronic coupling between the valence bands in this structure. Notably, this effect significantly improves with increasing pressure within the initially metallic phase, and its enhancement is even more prominent when considering the electron-phonon coupling between the valence bands, especially due to the hydrogen mass variation, whereas the impact of the sulfur isotope is relatively minimal. Additionally, the sulfur isotope effect contributes negatively while the hydrogen isotopes contribute positively, indicating that the sulfur effect dominates at lower pressures, but the hydrogen effect becomes prominent and dominates at higher pressures. These computational results predict that the isotopic effect in H$_{3}$S will exhibit a nonmonotonic pressure dependence, and the coefficient $\beta$ will become significantly larger at higher pressures, eventually surpassing the value predicted for hydrogen at zero pressure, and may even surpass the value predicted for muon-based superconductors at very high pressures.

In evolutionary biology, average gene substitution rates are often compared to phenotypic changes by assuming a linear relationship. However, for gene substitutions with non-negligible effects, this is not generally the case. We investigate the average effect of a gene substitution on the population's phenotypic distribution, considering infinite site models with mutations of various types and distributions. A key finding is that the average effect of a gene substitution is proportional to the average phenotypic change for infinitesimal mutations, but it diverges from linearity for larger mutations. Mathematical formulas for the average effect are developed for continuous and discrete scenarios, along with a method to estimate the average effect from genetic variation within populations. To illustrate the significance of our work, we discuss the implications for understanding the dynamics of emerging mutations during speciation, the responsiveness of developmental genes, and the accuracy of language models representing genetic information.

This study proposes a feedback control system for a bipedal robot's closed-loop feedback control. The framework is based on the idea that the robot's environment and movement dynamics can be viewed as a biological system undergoing meta-learning through reinforcement. The system utilizes feedback control to track a specific trajectory, with adjustments made to comply with impact dynamics during gait cycles. The feedback control system offers a novel approach to treating bipedal locomotion as a predictable process that can be managed and adapted to various environments, consistent with the principles of open-loop feedback control observed in human gait dynamics. The research involves a feedback control system designed for a specific bipedal robot model to maintain balance and move forward, with simulations demonstrating its effectiveness in coping with unexpected disturbances and navigating diverse terrain.

Our approach combines state-of-the-art learned descriptor methods with classic RANSAC-based pose estimation techniques, leveraging local and global features to estimate camera position. Localized deep descriptors are used in close-range scenarios and global descriptors are employed for longer-range calculations. Our novel learning method integrates camera constraints into the training process of deep descriptors to refine predictions in challenging environments. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, which outperforms or matches the performance of state-of-the-art methods while demonstrating enhanced reliability in difficult scenarios. Our code and model will be made available.

In the personalization domain, a distinct approach within federated learning, a central server supplies clients with personalized models through incremental gradient descent. However, this technique is hampered by the assumption that certain clients have access to unlimited unlabeled data and high computing power. To overcome this challenge, our novel semi-supervised learning technique is rooted in the assumption that each client has a limited dataset with unique, manually labeled data. By utilizing this labeled information, our research introduces a personalized semi-supervised learning paradigm, known as the Distilled Asymmetric Teacher-Student (DATS), that enhances the learning capabilities of clients. By incorporating data augmentation and instance-level classification, our DATS technique expands the virtual student's dataset, allowing it to generalize better. Furthermore, our Distilled DATS (DDATS) variant utilizes knowledge distillation to improve the learning performance of clients by incorporating labels from the virtual student. Our experiments, conducted across multiple datasets, demonstrate that our DATS and DDATS techniques outperform current, state-of-the-art personalization methods.

The decomposition of a neutron star is a critical phase in binary neutron star mergers. This process involves the disruption of the star and the reorganization of its magnetic field within the accretion disk formed from the initial matter. A crucial aspect of this event is the transformation of the magnetic field, which expands and becomes tangled upon destruction, leading to a significant decrease in electron collisionality within the disk. Through the use of MHD simulations in a spherical coordinate system, researchers have explored the dynamic response of the disk and investigated how this event impacts the spiral arm patterns and radiation patterns of the post-merger system.

We've demonstrated that for a smooth projective curve over a non-algebraically closed field, the first Mumford-Morita-Miller class can be defined as a element of a specific cohomology group. This result has consequences for understanding mapping class groups and vector bundles on such curves. These findings also have implications for understanding moduli spaces of line bundles and vector bundles, especially in the case of mixed characteristic.

This study establishes specific conditions on a Markov process so that it has a unique quasi-stationary distribution that converges exponentially, under the assumption that its suspension with respect to any open set has a unique stationary measure supported within that set. Our results are applied to verify the conditions for a large category of processes, including discrete-time Markov chains and continuous-time Markov processes, and the findings are illustrated with concrete examples.

Within a chemical potential range where graphene's charge carriers behave like relativistic particles, the equilibrium positions of particles in an electric field are influenced by their charge type and chemical potential. Graphene's properties allow for the variation of its chemical potential through interaction with residual dops or via the injection of carriers from a probe. We demonstrate that precisely controlling this chemical potential can force charged particles into predetermined patterns, thereby facilitating the development of novel nano- and microelectromechanical systems.

To identify the optimal Emergency Department (ED) stay duration, we studied the trade-offs between treating patients and freeing up space, known as the 'bed occupancy problem.' Using a cost-effectiveness analysis, we considered the cost of providing treatment now against potential adverse outcomes and costs resulting from prolonged ED stay. Adapting a framework by van den Bos, et al., we estimated the cost of providing treatment per patient and weighted it against the probability of the patient experiencing adverse outcomes, such as revisiting the ED or being hospitalized within thirty days. These probabilities were derived from a retrospective cohort study involving 49,778 patients at a single hospital in Boston. We applied the framework in a hypothetical scenario, reducing the time patients spent in the ED by 30 minutes, to determine the cost-balance point. This revealed that increasing the realized treatment time by 30 minutes resulted in a decrease in both ED revisit and readmission rates. Specifically, we observed a 4.5% decrease in ED revisit rate and a 3.4% decrease in readmission rate. Our findings suggest that extending the ED stay duration could yield beneficial outcomes, reducing both direct and indirect costs associated with adverse outcomes. These results have implications for hospital policymakers, advising them to consider treating patients for longer to mitigate the pressure of bed occupancy, although the optimal duration remains uncertain.

In moldovan's influential paper, a dilemma posed by a multi-agent system's complexity led to the conclusion that a particular solution requires an exponentially complex computation to achieve, prompting speculation about the potential of other solutions. We refute this claim by demonstrating that a less computationally demanding approach can yield the desired outcome. Building on prior research regarding task difficulty distributions, our argument hinges on specific characteristics of these distributions rather than the individual tasks themselves, presenting a hypothesis regarding the beneficial effects of difficulty variability. Through simulation-based verification, our findings indicate that this approach is both effective and desirable, likely to be preferred by the agents themselves. Consequently, this methodology should be considered the optimal solution.

Research focuses on understanding the link between two- and four-particle collisions and local charge conservation, with findings related to quark-gluon plasma and atomic collisions. Specifically, we examine how collective flow effects, derived from single-particle distributions, impact the measurements of charge-dependent correlations. It's discovered that the four-particle correlation measurement of volume and spatial anisotropies is influenced by the same biases as two-particle correlations, leading to increased uncertainties. However, this correlation can be corrected. Furthermore, our study reveals that how particles are arranged in space is influenced by the impact of collective flow on both two- and four-particle correlations. It's discovered that this impact results in an underestimation of collisional zone dimensions by approximately 30%. In contrast, the imaginary part of the loss per color charge is accurately determined across all centralities. Our study confirms that higher-order correlations provide valuable insights, despite being sensitive to different system properties. Ultimately, a comprehensive understanding of all correlations is necessary to uncover the truths of particle collisions.

This study introduces a novel approach to forecast project fundraising outcomes
based on crowd dynamics, analyzing the interactions within online communities.
Building on prior research, which primarily relied on static project attributes,
our method considers the temporal nature of crowd behavior and its influence on
project success. By comparing the crowd's features to those of individual projects and
their creators, our model discovers patterns that enable the prediction of fundraising
outcomes. Evaluations on a dataset from GitHub revealed that the proposed model
outperforms a baseline solution, which uses the project creators' profiles to forecast
performance. Furthermore, our method produces an attention matrix that provides
valuable insights into the relevance of crowd behavior to fundraising outcomes.

In the realm of digital forensics and cybersecurity, innovative techniques are necessary to tackle complex problems. A key challenge lies in developing models that balance efficiency with privacy and data security. The integration of federated learning, a decentralized machine learning approach, and digital forensics offers promising prospects. Motivated by the need to improve cybersecurity, this paper brings together FL and network intrusion detection systems. A novel intrusion detection framework, based on FL and deep neural networks, is developed to help organizations collaborate privately in identifying intrusions. This framework allows each organization to train its local model and share updated parameters securely via encrypted updates. As a result, each organization receives a global model tailored to its data, without exposing it to others. Additionally, this framework includes a novel evaluation method to determine when a new, unfamiliar attack is detected. Using the 2018 Carnegie Mellon University-acquired Network Intrusion Synthesis System, as well as the 2019-2020 datasets from the University of New South Wales, this framework demonstrates its effectiveness in identifying known attacks with a high degree of accuracy and sets a new standard for detection accuracy for uncommon attacks.

Online learning of robotic tasks like picking and packing demands just-in-time task planning. Nevertheless, the standard resolution strategies employed in research forums, such as planning via search, face issues related to high computational needs and execution constraints due to their exponential nature. In many robotic applications, specifically in processing and manufacturing, the successive tasks often exhibit a spatial or temporal connection. To take advantage of this dependency, we suggest an optimal linear time approach for solving just-in-time task planning problems by exploiting coarsity properties, resulting in faster execution times. Our approach results in an orthogonal basis that allows for the successive decomposition of a large search problem into simpler subtasks, ultimately yielding a more efficient solution. Our method, when tested on a variety of robotic tasks with dependency, achieves a substantial speedup, specifically 100 to 1000 times faster, when compared to the traditional planning via search approach.

This research explores the potential of using metal-oxide-gate field-effect transistors fabricated using high-mobility materials, such as InGaZnO, to detect electrical signals from cells in an Microelectrode Array. To evaluate this concept, researchers conducted a study within a simulated microenvironment that mimics the conditions found in a real MIARA system. They tested the metal-oxides InGaZnO and MgZnO, as well as a reference gate made from n-type doped silicon, in order to assess which material is more effective at detecting electrical signals from cells and determining cell viability. After treating the cells with an antibiotic that causes them to die, researchers used an electrostatic method to move them closer to the gate and then measuring the current change to determine cell count. The results showed that the high-mobility metal-oxides can detect cellular signals with precision similar to that of the silicon gate, while also demonstrating potential ways to improve detection.

We investigated the stability of complex systems consisting of interconnected oscillators within a ring structure, where each oscillator received information about the phase averages in the network. Despite having identical local interaction rules, the oscillators were arranged in groups, each with distinct system parameters. For systems with small deviations from ideal conditions, we developed a theory by utilizing a mean-field approach and applying the methods of bifurcation analysis and normal form reductions. This approach allowed us to create a predictive framework for determining the critical boundaries under perfect and chaotic group synchronization. Our analysis revealed how system parameter variability affects the stability of these synchronization states and how it influences the survival of the oscillating groups under certain correlation and population size conditions. Moreover, we demonstrated that an optimal population size exists for each correlation level, offering a means to optimize group synchronization.

Our research examines the dominance of YouTube within the global multimedia search landscape. To achieve this, we centered our investigation on 13 prominent search engines operating in Western, Eastern, and Middle/North African regions. Our analysis via screenshots captured monthly search engine snapshots revealed a noticeable pattern: YouTube was consistently outputted in search results for queries involving music but was frequently omitted from searches containing film titles. Notably, this pattern recurring across multiple search engines highlighted YouTube's prominent role in film-related searches. Our study shows that YouTube's inclusion in search queries is not only common but also influenced by the search engine's overall performance, featuring in roughly 30% of all relevant film searches.

We've developed an approach to apply the $\beta$-function methodology in models featuring various types of monodromy defects, extending beyond the realm of defect-free systems. Our methodology is flexible, accommodating novel defect representations and allows for an unified examination of their impact on the systems' behavior. Through this analysis, we can identify the regime in which the defects' effects are minimal, which in turn enables us to demonstrate the existence of a critical value for the coupling constant in these systems. Furthermore, our findings also imply the loss of bases in this context. To illustrate the accuracy and applicability of our approach, we provide a detailed account of a specific example involving a $\mathbb{CP}^1$ model interacting with a defect resembling a semi-infinite version of a lattice model known as the fuzzy sphere. Our calculations reveal a critical coupling constant and the loss of bases for a multitude of monodromy defects, the range of which extends from those with full $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ symmetry to a highly degenerate case in which the defects' effects are negligible.

We establish the local nonconjugation criterion for elliptic curves over a cubic extension with a rational point of order 13. Our proof combines recent findings from Bruinier and Kroukowski with Mumford's earlier work on level 13 elliptic surfaces.

The temporal characteristics of network devices are influenced by local delay, which is typically not considered in network topology analysis. In this research, we examine the effects of local delay on the part of SIP servers in wireless sensor networks, mapping out existence and uniqueness regions in terms of delay and network parameters. These findings are used to develop a model-based SIP server selection algorithm centered on the $N$-order Simpson rule, demonstrating through simulations that the proposed method outperforms existing SIP routing methods, particularly in terms of connection establishment speed.

Semi-supervised node classification in graph neural networks is often approached using a combination of training and pseudo-labeling techniques to expand labeling scope beyond initial training sets. However, methods such as mean-field and multi-step consistency pseudo-labeling have been shown to exacerbate node prediction errors and limit the effectiveness of these methods in large-scale graph neural networks. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel pseudo-labeling technique, known as self-enforced pseudo-labeling (SEL), both theoretically and practically. By enforcing consistency across different levels of network structures through a self-monitoring approach, SEL complements SGGN and improves its performance on various benchmark datasets.

Our research introduces PatchNet, a lightweight neural network framework for real-time object detection in videos. To create an efficient framework, we divide each pixel into multiple components and reduce the complexity of each component using a novel feature map representation. This innovative approach enhances computational speed while minimizing memory usage. We also adapt the framework to be applicable across various datasets and algorithms for object detection. After implementing the framework using mobile devices, our comparative analysis shows that PatchNet performs better than existing lightweight models, such as MobileNetV2, under similar computational constraints. Notably, PatchNet achieves higher Average Precision (AP) compared to MobileNetV2 by at least 10% on multiple datasets, including GOT-10k and Caltech Pedestrian, in both one-shot and multi-shot training scenarios. Our experiments further confirm that PatchNet offers higher accuracy and faster inference speed than other existing efficient detectors on various video datasets. Finally, our analysis demonstrates that PatchNet's accuracy remains consistent even when dealing with novel videos.

This research investigates how varying initial conditions and system parameters affect multiple distribution functions for a discrete time version of the TASEP model with multiple particles at different sites. Unlike most studies on this topic, which focus on distributions centered at zero, this study examines distributions both above and below the average particle position. We develop an operator-valued difference equation to represent these multi-point distributions. This approach builds on prior research by Gier and Mojtabai, which focused on a single distribution function (namely, the distribution above the average particle position) and proved it converges under certain conditions. Under the assumption that system parameters are stable (i.e., they do not increase indefinitely over time), we demonstrate that multi-point distributions converge and develop explicit formulas for them. Notably, we find that system dynamics affect some of these distributions more strongly than others. Additionally, we define certain combination weights and demonstrate that a system in a stationary state will have distributions that are both upper and lower bounds for systems in non-stationary states with similar initial conditions but varying system parameters.

This study investigates the challenges and opportunities presented by a SWIPT-enabled wireless communication network with energy constraints on both the access and backhaul links. To efficiently balance energy harvesting and data transmission, we introduce the generalized antenna-switching technique, combining with time-switching and power-switching modes. This allows us to devise an optimal resource allocation strategy, focusing on maximizing the long-term system weight and energy efficiency. We employ a stochastic joint optimization framework, accounting for their respective powers on the access and backhaul links, and consider a base station with multiple tiers and multiple users. By leveraging a compact representation via a stochastic variable and utilizing a Q-learning based algorithm, we propose a solution that dynamically adjusts switching variables. This enables us to achieve a trade-off between system efficiency and simplicity in implementation. Furthermore, we examine the asymptotic performance of the proposed algorithm and demonstrate its efficacy through extensive simulation results, showcasing its superiority over alternative schemes.

In this study, a comprehensive perturbative calculation for SU(N) fermions in (1+1)d to the fourth-order has been performed, achieving an accurate analytical result. Surprisingly, fourth-order perturbation theory aligns with second-order results in some aspects, particularly in excited states, while yielding distinct outcomes in ground state energy. To address this discrepancy, a variable renormalization scheme is introduced, enabling a detailed analysis of the perturbative ground state and its implications for binding lengths. Furthermore, this theoretical framework has been applied to solve the mass spectrum of mesonic systems, namely baryons and mesons, and the limits of infinite N color degeneracy have been thoroughly investigated.

In the standard quantum treatment of optomechanics, the motion of a single particle is described by a harmonic oscillator, where the quantum aspects become negligible when occupation numbers exceed 100. However, this method is not suitable for studying the collective motion of many particles, for which there is no established quantum treatment. We introduce a new approach, grounded in classical electric circuit models, to address this gap. Surprisingly, this method reveals significant quantum effects, even for immense occupation numbers in the classical regime. This unforeseen phenomenon is particularly pronounced in systems with multiple coupled oscillators, where quantum entanglement leads to lasting correlations among the motion of all particles, even in the classical domain.

On the real line, Jacobi polynomials are classical orthogonal polynomials, defined by a weight $w(x)$ and normalized to have zero constant term. By considering limits, Freud weights and Hermite--Hubbard weights are obtained from Jacobi polynomials, while Airy weights arise from a different limiting process. This paper examines generalized sextic Freud and Airy weights, providing details on their development, a comparison between them, and specific weights obtained when certain parameters are constrained.

This research focuses on how a robot moving along a wall adjusts its distance from the wall, using only a narrow-field-of-view sensor, to detect a target, such as a nearby door, within that view. Based on this detection, the robot needs to decide whether to take a shortcut or stick to its original wall-following path. Our key finding shows that the robot's decision-making strategy depends heavily on its field of view and wall-following sensor's range, leading to situations where the robot needs to trade off its distance from the wall to complete this task successfully. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the robot must maintain a minimum safe distance from the wall to successfully take the shortcut, a crucial consideration for wall-following robots.

This paper focuses on perturbative algebraic quantum field theory from the perspective of covariant components. We aim to demonstrate that the restrictions imposed by a specific Cauchy surface can be avoided in defining subalgebras, thereby making the theory's causality aspects more understandable. Furthermore, we provide a simplified interpretation of renormalizable interactions and their expansions in perturbation theory, facilitating the identification of observables in the theory.

To address the issue of false negatives in the detection of smoke images, we introduce an image enhancement technique combining SmokeNet. This method, called SmokeEnhancer, actively amplifies smoke images and suppresses non-smoke images. By combining SmokeEnhancer with SmokeNet, we can improve the robustness of the system and decrease false negatives. Through experiments using a smoke-free AI-assisted laparoscope system, we discovered that SmokeEnhancer successfully elevates the smoke score of genuine smoke images while lowering the score of non-smoke images. Consequently, the overall accuracy of the system was enhanced. Notably, the precision of smoke detection increased more significantly than the precision of false positives. Hence, we propose a algorithm called precision-recall differential (PRD), defined as the variation in precision relative to the variation in recall in a specific direction, to evaluate the effectiveness of image enhancement techniques.

We introduce a novel method for creating a robust M\"olmer-Sorensen gate using a 31-ion chain by combining frequency modulation and a specific design approach. This results in a gate with a high level of frequency tolerance while maintaining its coherence. Our research showcases the importance of ion placement and frequency design in achieving a robust M\"olmer-Sorensen gate. Using numerical simulations, we examine the impact of variable frequency fluctuations, resulting in a gate that remains stable within $\pm 500$ mHz, and is capable of generating a significant amount of entanglement within a few seconds, and up to ten qubits, without exhibiting a speed limit. This innovation paves the way for the development of more complex quantum algorithms on ion chains.

Our study employs first-principles simulations to analyze the structural aspects of several ABO3 perovskites. The research focuses on how the equilibrium volume and presence of B-cation off-centering in these materials are affected by the size of the A cation. The results reveal that off-centering in the B cation is influenced by both the A cation size and the lattice volume, with larger A cations typically resulting in greater off-centering. Additionally, our findings for PbTiO3 and HfTiO5 agree with experimental data, while also providing new insights. The study also examines the material's ferroelectric behavior, finding that off-centering along different axes in the lattice is distinct and potentially leads to different material properties and phase transitions.

In this research, we introduce a new multivariate Gaussian process framework that incorporates conditional independence constraints into the statistical model. This technique is ideal for predicting multiple data sets, such as stock prices or medical measurements, under specific graphical relationships where individual processes are independent from one another given certain variables. By utilizing stochastic processes on directed graphs with marked nodes, our method can be seen as a combination of traditional Gaussian processes and vector-valued stochastic processes governed by kernel representations. This approach allows us to derive a novel kernel representation that captures the conditional independence relations between individual processes, thereby relaxing the traditional requirement for joint distributions in Gaussian models. Through scale mixtures of multivariate Stieltjes transforms, we establish a method for constructing specifiable covariance functions, including the innovation kernel, which enables the extension of Gaussian process regression to multiple data sets under specified graphical relationships. Furthermore, our method comes with computational efficient and scalable algorithms for posterior inference and prediction.

Recent breakthroughs in quantum circuit layers have led to remarkable accuracy in predicting molecular ground states, but the resource costs associated with computing excited states and molecular properties remain steep. We demonstrate how applying recurring quantum circuit patterns in depth can mitigate this expense. These patterns enhance the convergence of energy calculations and efficiently render simple, localized aspects of molecular properties. Moreover, we showcase a full-scale proof-of-concept example involving the computation of dipole moments via constrained path integral propagation of wave functions. We anticipate that our findings will encourage the development of more effective and compact recurrent quantum circuit patterns for future quantum computers.

A new iteration method called the Generalized Chebyshev method is developed, allowing for fast average-case convergence for a broad range of functions that are iteratively searchable. The method surpasses traditional gradient descent in achieving average-case convergence, matching its worst-case performance, while remaining computationally efficient and simple to implement. Unlike other optimization methods, the Generalized Chebyshev method achieves average-case convergence for non-convex functions, all while ensuring iteratively searchable criteria are met. Furthermore, the method remains insensitive to data noise, ensuring it remains effective even in challenging real-world scenarios. The study demonstrates the efficacy of the Generalized Chebyshev method across various applications, including least squares problems, deep learning, and network design.

Moiré heterostructures composed of twisted layers of transition metal dichalcogenides have exhibited unique properties resulting from their geometric and electronic characteristics. The formation of moiré patterns depends on the twist angles between adjacent layers and their size is typically in the order of nanometers, which is comparable to or larger than the interlayer distance. This study focuses on the optical phenomena in these structures and the effects of interlayer exciton exchange on their spectra. The results show that the interlayer exciton binding energy has a significant impact on the optical responses, and a greater binding energy leads to distinct optical features in the low-energy range. Conversely, a smaller binding energy causes fusion with higher-energy single-layer excitons, resulting in altered optical responses. The exchange of excitons between layers is also influenced by the moiré potential size and the direction of the twist angle, which in turn affects the band structure of these materials. The results of this study can serve as a foundation for predicting and analyzing various excitonic phenomena in moiré heterostructures and their applications in optoelectronics.

This research focuses on developing a versatile and efficient adaptive algorithm to mitigate the impact of measurement noise and model discrepancies on a mobile agent's navigation. Introduced is a novel probabilistic data association algorithm capable of adapting to changing scenarios without prior knowledge of dynamics. We demonstrate the proposed ADPDA's ability to overcome static assumptions and dynamically adjust to account for the agent's state change and external factors. Key features of the ADPDA include its ability to update Kalman gain variables through a self-correcting mechanism, utilizing historical data to refine estimates and reduce uncertainty. Furthermore, ADPDA's performance is not adversely affected by the presence of outliers, making it suitable for real-world applications. We thoroughly evaluate the ADPDA's performance in various scenarios through simulation and experimental analysis, comparing its results to state-of-the-art methods.

ATLAS has cooperated with CMS to conduct an in-depth examination of both polarized and
transverse states of $W$ and $Z$ bosons, resulting from the decay of a bottom quark.
This was achieved by jointly analyzing up to 1.1 fb$^{-1}$ of $W$ boson and 0.73 fb$^{-1}$
of $Z$ boson data collected in 2011. By comparing the $W$ boson decay rate patterns
for different polarization states, considering both helicities and transverse components,
ATLAS and CMS have simultaneously measured the helicity fractions. These measurements
are in line with Standard Model predictions. A notable observation in this study is
that the $Z$ boson decay patterns showed no visible difference between polarized and
transverse states, while the $W$ boson decay patterns exhibited a minor disparity.
These measurements are in harmony with Standard Model predictions.

A novel, locally Lorentz-invariant framework for a spin-3 particle is established, allowing for the construction of a representation-free, gauge-invariant Lagrangian. The model incorporates 3-spin symmetry as a natural consequence, and we determine the representation for a spin-3 particle within this context. The representation's properties allow for the creation of a representation-free, gauge-invariant action, which describes a spin-3 particle in a gravity field. Furthermore, we investigate both the scalar and spin-2 particle models within this setup, and demonstrate that our newly developed action for a spin-3 particle in a gravity field can be derived from a variational principle. Our work also reveals that the Cotton tensor serves as the source of the spin-3 particle's mass term in this framework, implying the spin-3 particle's vacuum state is equivalent to a special kind of conformal field state.

We establish a one-to-one correspondence between specific types of lattices and orthomodular spaces, providing a unified framework that encompasses several key mathematical structures. By means of this correspondence, various mathematical concepts can be interpreted and their interconnections explored. As a case in point, certain operations on these structures prove to be equivalently expressive, whereas others differ significantly. The established correlation also reveals novel relationships between certain mathematical concepts.

Recent advancements in legal reasoning research from a computational perspective have focused on developing systems that both understand and generate legal arguments. Although initially aimed at improving human review processes, the primary objective of systems built in this research area has been to mimic human-style proof development. This goal was achieved by incorporating system-generated proofs into the review process, specifically in applications involving legal aid for individuals (AILs). However, a critical challenge remains unresolved: the lack of a comprehensive theory or system for representing the outcomes of both human and system-generated proof activities. In the absence of such a representation, it is impossible to accomplish the primary goal of this research area, which is to facilitate the integration of system-generated proofs into the review process. This article presents a solution to this problem by introducing a representation framework that encodes the results of both human and system-generated proofs. We will demonstrate the efficacy of this representation, known as Legal Molecular Networks (LMNs), in two ways. Firstly, we will showcase its application in a system designed to generate proofs, which was initially developed by M.meta, a leading legal AI company. Secondly, we will illustrate its effectiveness in a system for automatic legal reasoning that we created. In both cases, the proposed representation will be shown to facilitate the seamless integration of system-generated proofs into the review process. Finally, we will discuss how this representation can be utilized in both system-generated and human-generated proof activities.

We explore the fourth moment of L-functions for cubic fields, motivated by Watson's seminal work, which initially considered the second moment. Our approach leverages Soundararajan and Harper's groundbreaking results on the third moment and the central limit theorem for L-function shifts. The derivation of the fourth moment involves a novel application of the fundamental lemma, combined with an analysis of the cubic field Sato-Tate measure.

Interior-point methods, a class of iterative techniques widely used to solve linear programming and quadratic programming problems, consist of four core steps. To enhance their performance, researchers have been exploring various ways to optimize these steps and improve efficiency. This study focuses on an innovative approach to the most computationally intensive step, involving a matrix decomposition technique that results in significant termination benefits with minimal impact on accuracy. This outcome is attributed to the specialized termination criteria developed as part of the analysis.
