The integration of data-driven techniques is revolutionizing the field of incident detection and classification in grid management. Specifically, advanced data analysis is helping utilities identify issues, such as power outages and system anomalies, in distribution networks more efficiently. This research focuses on developing a real-time incident detection and classification system for grids with energy storage systems (ESS) using operational data. A two-part classification technique, comprising decision tree-based and clustering analyses, is employed to identify incidents and determine their severity. A detailed evaluation is conducted using simulated data sets, including a large public data set (IEEE-39), to demonstrate how various classification methods and error metrics perform under different operating conditions. Our findings show that certain combinations of classification techniques and error metrics can outperform others in detecting incidents and accurately determining severity, particularly when analyzing distributed load patterns. In contrast, other cases, such as a reference trajectory-based approach, are more effective at distinguishing between incident and non-incident events. This study contributes to the existing literature on incident detection and classification in distribution grids with integrated energy storage systems, providing valuable insights for grid operators and managers.

Our research explores the radiative decays of the X(3872) state, specifically its two-body radiative decays into J/psi and two-pion or two-photon states. A reduced amplitude description, derived from nonrelativistic quark model calculations, is used to analyze the branching ratios and polarization correlations in X(3872) decays. Our study indicates that radiative decays into J/psi and photon pairs dominate the pattern of decay widths. Moreover, calculations show that the contributions of rho and omega mesons are relatively close, but the omega contribution is about 2.5 times greater than the rho contribution. It's found that the ratio of omega to rho contribution is roughly 2.5, resulting from the differing phase space volumes. Our research also predicts that the X(3872) decay into J/psi and a photon and a neutral pion will likely be its primary radiative decay channel, with a estimated decay width of approximately 1.5 times 10^-5. This analysis may help resolve the longstanding uncertainty regarding the decay width of the X(3872) state into J/psi and two photons.

A quadric's definition in projective space is established as having a definite inner product for which linear transformations that preserve the product are a subgroup of the vector space's general linear group. It's proven that smooth quadrics can be classified based on their Picard group and a specific divisor, which represents the quadric's intermediate subbundles of rank one. Known smooth quadrics are listed along with their respective invariants, and it's shown that any smooth quadric can be expressed as a union of hyperbolas defined by a specific polynomial, which is known as the Pfaffian.

We are thrilled to introduce TextWorldExpress, a revolutionary new version of the popular learning from demonstrations benchmark for text-based games. Since its initial launch in 2017, the benchmark has spurred a surge in innovative research and has become a staple in the community of text-based game learning. Over the years, advancements in the benchmark have been made through open calls for contribution, resulting in significant improvements. For example, the integration of Level 1 datasets from real games such as Montezuma's Revenge has set a new benchmark, leading to a substantial 250x increase in throughput. We believe that TextWorldExpress brings the benchmark into a new era of efficiency and effectiveness, offering new possibilities for evaluation and research.

To investigate how edge dislocations influence the electronic behavior of 3D Topological Insulators, we developed a theoretical framework that takes into account the influence of dislocations as well as their surface effects. Using the ATOTAKU method within the PyTZ code, we found that a screw dislocation in a 3D Topological Insulator leads to the formation of a closed loop of electron accumulation, with the dislocation axis aligned with the screw direction. Additionally, we discovered that a normal dislocation results in distinct electronic properties, including the presence of Hall bars and the divergence of the electrostatic potential at the core, leading to electron and hole distributions that could be confined in this area. Our research suggests that these closed loops and surface interactions may provide a means to detect and observe dislocations in 3D Topological Insulators.

The research explores $p$-harmonic functions within the semilatus rectus domain $R_+ \times \Omega$ and $\Omega \times R_+$. Here, $\Omega$ is a simply connected, bounded domain in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $n \geq 2$, and we investigate how the parameter $p$ affects the uniqueness of these functions. We demonstrate that if $p > 1$ causes the Dirichlet $p$-Laplace operator to be elliptic, we can establish the uniqueness of its positive solutions. Consequently, this investigation leads to significant implications for the fractional Laplacian and the Hardy operator. Our analysis also reveals a unique nondegenerate positive solution to the fractional Laplacian in the half-space $R_+ \times \Omega$, given that $p = \frac{n+2}{n}$, and we identify a critical value of $p$ that influences nonuniqueness in the domain $\Omega \times R_+$.

Highly correlated large-scale weather patterns, identified through satellite wind speed data, result in significant wind forces and wave interactions along sea surfaces. When extreme weather conditions occur, they tend to cause severe impacts, including damage to structures and loss of life. Understanding the spatial extent of extreme weather is crucial; however, current research lacks thorough analysis in this area.

By utilizing a data-driven approach, this study examines the substantial wind forces and wave interactions during extreme weather conditions. Using satellite data from Metop, researchers calculated the distance over which extreme weather patterns' effects decayed when conditioned on extremely high wind speeds. The findings revealed decay distances of approximately 3000 to 4000 kilometers for wind speed and around 2000 kilometers for wave height. These numbers demonstrate the spatial reach of extreme weather patterns, emphasizing the necessity of considering these patterns in risk assessments and damage predictions.

We provide a straightforward proof that hyperbolicity of a minimal face of the cone of effective divisors of degree $d$ on a toric variety implies the existence of $O(\sqrt{\log d})$ rational points of height $\sqrt{d}$. This confirms a recent conjecture of Bußing. As a byproduct, our argument also confirms the existence of multiple rational points of similar height on certain subvarieties, thus demonstrating the abundance of rational points on certain log-Fano varieties. This is a toric analogue of a recent result obtained by Przyjawski.

The widespread use of Lie groups in various applications has given rise to a need for matrix manipulability on related manifolds. Building upon the work of Schaummann et al. (2021), this paper expands the concept of manipulability to Riemannian manifolds, offering a geometric interpretation of manipulability matrices or ellipsoids. The paper then develops specific formulas for manipulability on matrices from Lie groups, orthogonal matrices, and Grassmann manifolds. The paper also presents algorithms for computing these manipulability matrices or ellipsoids. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of these algorithms through geometric optimization problems, including motion planning and image registration.

Theoretical predictions for electroweak Higgs boson production in association with a top quark pair at the LHC, considering the presence of top quark pair production, are within 10% accuracy for current experimental measurements, using the next-to-leading order perturbative QCD framework and the matching of parton shower simulations. A comparable level of accuracy, -5% to -15%, can be achieved at the third-order using the fixed-order calculation for the Higgs boson transverse momentum distribution, alone or in combination with the next-to-leading order perturbative QCD prediction. These predictions are expected to be sufficiently accurate for the analysis of experimental data in the future LHC runs.

A novel 3D object estimation model, called CoCa, has been proposed. It leverages a multi-stage training approach, first training separate models for distinct views and then combining these into a single robust CoCa model through target projection training. This unique training method enhances the learning of canonical poses. Additionally, a novel generalization metric was developed for 3D object estimation models and used to assess various existing models, including ImageNet-LV2, MuCo, and NeoMoCo. Through this analysis, it was discovered that existing models failed the new generalization test. In response, a new dataset, called MinMuCo, was created with minimal mixing to better evaluate the robustness of 3D object estimation models. Finally, it was demonstrated that CoCa, trained on MuCo and MinMuCo, surpasses all other existing models in terms of novel view accuracy while significantly improving canonical pose learning.

Despite widespread agreement on the need for countermeasures against vaccine-related misinformation, researchers have yet to develop a comprehensive framework for comprehending and predicting such misinformation. Our approach, called the Attitudes Toward Vaccine-Related Disinformation Framework (AVRDF), identifies critical factors that contribute to and can be predicted from public perceptions of vaccine-related misinformation. This framework, built on prior knowledge, includes components such as users' critical thinking, motivation to cope with misinformation, belief in vaccination, and prior knowledge. By leveraging AVRDF, we can shape counterstrategies such as designing misinformation detection apps that accurately work for every user. Our findings demonstrate that these apps will only be effective for a significant number of users if they are specifically tailored for each individual or group within the vast Twitter audience. This research highlights the intricacies of vaccine-related misinformation and provides novel insights that can guide strategy development in the battle against all types of online disinformation.

Producing attosecond pulses with specified central energy and brief temporal duration is crucial for numerous scientific and technological applications. Our study demonstrates that attosection pulses from a molecular target can be precisely crafted by adjusting the target's alignment to align a specific atomic subshell with the linear polarization of the driving laser, thus enhancing or suppressing high-harmonic generation. This way, we can control the central energy and temporal duration of the attosecond pulses. Our findings are confirmed by experiments using scanning near-field optical microscopy and supported by theoretical models and computations.

We've conducted an extensive analysis of the binary system Algol C, using high-precision photometric data collected over a period of 125 years. Despite claims that its orbital period is increasing, our research reveals that it remains constant and accurate to a precision of 0.5 milliseconds. To test the system's stability, we employed a spectral analysis, finding that it is free from significant trends or outliers for the past 25 years. By determining the characteristics of its variability, we found that it is primarily driven by the eclipsing process and a small residual effect related to the uneven distribution of light from its components.

Investigating the boundary-induced blow-up in the Schrödinger equation involves considering a specific scenario: a Schrödinger equation that incorporates both time (t) and space (x) variables and includes a constant coefficient (c) and initial conditions that cause the solution to experience exponential growth in time, specifically the solution to the equation $i\partial_t u = \Delta u + c|D^\alpha|u$. However, since this equation's classical methods of proving blow-up are bounded by assuming certain conditions, an alternative approach is taken to demonstrate the boundary-induced blow-up for a specific set of parameters (c, α). This approach is capable of handling certain ranges of (c, α) and is an extension of previous work by Biazin and Biazin-Da-Costa, which investigated the case where the derivative exponent α is 2, and the boundary conditions were omitted. Additionally, when the exponent α is 2, the resulting equation can be transformed into the one-dimensional nonlinear Schrödinger equation, and its blow-up boundary conditions can be derived from previous research on the equation $i\partial_t u = \Delta u + cu$.

Deep Network PINNs trained using Monte Carlo sampling suffer from low training efficiency due to infrequently activated network layers and slow gradient propagation. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Residual-based Adaptive Node Generation method, which dynamically creates new network nodes, thereby accelerating PINN training. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our RANG method in reducing training time for PINNs, with a notable improvement of 97.6% without any loss in testing accuracy. Additionally, RANG maintains satisfactory performance even in challenging conditions, such as large network depths, and its source code has been made publicly available.

Our analysis of electron flow through iron-bearing ferroelectric field-effect transistors takes into account the ferroelectric material's domain structure. By combining the Landau theory of ferroic order with a simple electron flow model, we determine how the ferroelectric's periodic crystal structure affects conduction band patterns. This leads to a more detailed understanding of how the ferroelectric's polarization affects electron flow, which is essential for accurately predicting the impact of ferroelectric domain structure on iron-based ferroelectric field-effect transistor performance.

Our previous research revealed that many libraries in the Rust ecosystem harbored vulnerabilities, however, the situation seemed somewhat dire. We decided to delve deeper and investigate how the situation has evolved over time. Our analysis of Cargo's dependency database revealed both positive and negative outcomes. On a positive note, the majority of libraries have addressed security issues and upgraded to fix existing vulnerabilities. Conversely, a significant proportion of libraries still expose vulnerabilities in their most recent versions, posing a risk to applications that use them. Moreover, many developers continue to rely on outdated, security-flawed versions of libraries, albeit in a diminished capacity. These findings suggest that while progress has been made, there remains a pressing need for improved security awareness and secure development practices in the Rust community.

This research investigates the long-term behavior of stochastic complex Ginzburg-Laudau equations, driven by various types of noise, either continuously or in discrete time jumps. The analysis focuses on the average impact, both spatially and temporally, that pure jump noises have on the system's ergodic properties. The findings have important implications for determining necessary conditions for system ergodicity. The theoretical predictions are substantiated by numerical simulations. The study particularly addresses the instance where the jump noise affects only a subset of the system's components, potentially resembling a situation encountered in light-sensitive systems. The work is registered in arXiv's physics category, specifically within physics.stat mech.

Let $G$ be a finite noncyclic abelian group, with $G$ not being isomorphic to either $\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$ or $\mathbb{Z}_{pq}$ for prime numbers $p$ and $q$. We have previously established that the minimum degree in the power graph of $G$ is at most $\sqrt{|G|}$ for the case when $G$ is nilpotent of class two. In this current research, we determine the minimum degree in the power graph of a group $G$ when $G$ is nilpotent of class two but is not nilpotent by definition. We also present an analysis on the maximum degree in the power graph of a group $G$ when $G$ is nilpotent of class two but is not nilpotent by definition. We also present an analysis on the maximum degree in the power graph of a group $G$ when $G$ is nilpotent of class two. We also determine the minimum degree in the power graph of a group $G$ when $G$ is abelian but not nilpotent by definition.

Starting this summer, the LHC will begin its second data collection period with protons carrying higher energy levels, reaching 2.36 TeV per beam, a significant increase from the 2009-2010 tests. For comparison, the CERN's old ring, the ISS, had achieved 24 GeV per beam in the 1960s, a mere 1 million times less energy. This energy boost is crucial for confirming the Higgs boson theory and searching for supersymmetry and other rare phenomena. To handle the increased energy, researchers will utilize 20-meter-long, crumpled metal horns to focus the protons into 25-femtometer-wide beams, closely matching the predictions from computer simulations. However, actual construction of the horns was a complex challenge, particularly in getting the magnetic coils just right, as slight errors could cause significant beam divergence. In the end, the first prototype successfully matched the desired magnetic field pattern, allowing it to focus the protons at an accuracy of 1 meter, and production of the remaining horns is now underway.

Recent research has demonstrated that Gabor filters, derived from 2D Gaussians, 
excels in visual cortex mimicry and numerous applications that prioritize 
intermediate-level visual data. However, the conventional Gabor models prove 
ineffective when applied to tasks necessitating robustness to extreme orientation 
changes. To address this limitation, we suggest Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), 
an innovative family of Gabor filters whose scales are tied to key features 
in a neural network's input. This approach ensures that LGFs are robust to significant 
orientation changes and provide a reliable intermediate-level representation 
of visual data. We apply LGFs to the challenging problem of digit recognition 
in the MNIST dataset and show that LGFs significantly enhance the robustness 
and accuracy of deep neural networks across various tasks.

Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) are a fundamental class of graph neural networks that address a diverse set of applications. However, the implicit inductive biases embedded in GCNs, resulting from iteratively gathering neighbors from the local environment, pose limitations in modeling independent graph structure features. This limitation can be addressed through a novel GGN model, a new type of graph neural network, designed to uncouple graph feature gathering from the ordering process. By introducing a separate mechanism for shuffling the feature gathering order, the GGN model achieves two significant advantages. Firstly, it reduces the hidden representations learned at each layer, making it more computationally efficient. Secondly, it enables the model to learn graph features independently, without being influenced by the sequential order of previous layers. As a result, the GGN model offers two superior aspects - reduced computational complexity and more independent graph feature learning capabilities. Experimentally, the new model outperforms the conventional GCNs in multiple datasets, and its computational efficiency improves by at least 30%.

Researchers have utilized Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to create various types of attacks on neural networks, but these attacks require prior knowledge of the target model, making them difficult to execute in real-world scenarios. Additionally, existing attacks often introduce minimal noise, which is insufficient to disrupt the model's performance in many cases. In this research, we introduce a novel Trojan attack that can be executed successfully without prior knowledge of the target model and incorporate substantial noise, which can persist beyond the initial model and even affect subsequent models trained on the same data. Our attack, known as the false rumor spread Trojan attack, achieves high success rates of 94.8% and 99.9% for LRT and BRF noise types, respectively, while only requiring a limited number of model queries. Our methodology involves training two neural networks, where the first generates target labels based on input data and the second enhances noise levels based on the output of the first model, which is also refined by a discriminator. This unique approach enables the propagation of the Trojan attack, making it substantially more applicable in real-world scenarios. Our empirical evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of our attack, which cannot be thwarted by existing defense methods.

The Rosaceo Instrument with Integral Field (ROSIE IFU) is a unique, advanced optical system that produces a 3D data set of celestial objects' light patterns. This research showcases the ROSIE IFU's capabilities through its preliminary observations of several objects at the National Telescope of the University of Genova (NTUG). The NTUG's telescope, boasting a 0.8 meters primary mirror, is an ideal platform for the ROSIE IFu, allowing it to obtain spatial information across a 20.5 x 20.5 arcseconds field of view. Each pixel within this field delivers a spectrum, enabling the identification of objects extending 20.5 arcseconds in diameter. Our observations involve the following targets: the nebulae NGC 2024, NGC 2174, and NGC 2175; the galaxy Markarian 729, and the nebulae PNKAC 103, PNQ 1-2, and PNVEL 1 in the Caldwell Catalog. Data analysis involved calibrating raw data with standard software, utilizing a series of steps including dark current subtraction, removal of digital signals, and application of extraction algorithms. Following this, we obtained a data set ready for processing, which we presented as a final map. This research marked the ROSIE IFu's inaugural observations, showcasing its potential for spatial mapping, continuum intensity measurements, and emission line detection across various wavelengths.

This research presents combined experimental and theoretical findings on low-energy astrophysical $S$-factors for the $^{19}$F+p reaction. The study used multiple detection techniques to measure $\gamma$-ray yields resulting from specific nuclear state transitions following the $^{20}$Ne compound state unbinding. The derived $S$-factor values were calculated at specific energy intervals, and multiple theoretical models were utilized to model our data and predict behavior at lower energy levels. The results showed that at energies up to a few keV, our $S$-factor data matched well with existing data, and both experimental and theoretical models indicated that the $S$-factor would decrease by approximately 30% at energy levels just above our study's 92-keV threshold. This decrease is likely caused by the resonant nature of a low-lying $^{20}$Ne state in this energy range. Considering that this reaction is involved in specific stellar events, our study's results may impact our understanding of how these processes change the light element composition in such environments.

Scientists evaluated the constructible exoplanets within habitable zones of 50 close-by G-type dwarfs using data from Earth-based telescopes. They used Earth's mass and composition as a base case, then considered various alternative interior structures and rock-to-ice ratios. Even with these different configurations, researchers found it's extremely unlikely to find multiple Earth-like planets with similar compositions around any given star. However, they predict they can find several stars hosting single exo-Earths made primarily of rocky material with water present in the liquid form. In contrast, ice-dominated exo-Earths either get dehydrated or lose surface material due to gravitational interaction with their host star, ultimately failing to find a suitable host star. To increase their search, researchers recommend targeting G-type stars that are slightly older, as their age would allow sufficient time for these celestial bodies to form.

In large MIMO systems, channel state information is gathered through pilot signals. To enhance feature learning, we propose an attention-based mechanism for extracting crucial pilot data. The pilot performance is first assessed using an attention attention network, which prioritizes significant information and minimizes redundant data. The proposed attention-based channel extractor (ABCE) was compared with existing methods using numerical simulations on 5G datasets. The results indicate that ABCE reduces training data requirements by a factor of 10 and boosts its classification accuracy while also decreasing the model's parameter count.

In the realm of modal logic, the notion of a "possible world" is increasingly seen as a variable rather than a fixed concept. This dynamic perspective on worlds is embodied in the framework of topological categories. By projecting systems of accessible worlds within networks, we demonstrate that each topological category is associated with a specific modal topology. Conversely, every modal topology can be derived from a topological category defining the relationships between accessible worlds. This categorical approach to worlds is versatile and facilitates the analysis of multiple relationships between states of affairs. Moreover, we have introduced a method for deriving modal topological systems from first-order categorical logic, including the expansion of modal topological systems to accommodate basic lawlike sentences.

In 1990, Faudree and Schelp proposed a hypothesis stating that every bipartite graph with a maximum degree of 3 has a strong edge coloring that utilizes at most one more color than the minimum number required for an equitable coloring. By contrast, we present a bipartite graph with a maximum degree of 3 whose strong edge-coloring implementation surpasses its equitable coloring implementation in terms of color count.

Let $d$ be a positive integer. A graph with vertices as functions from a set $A$ to a set $B$, where a function $f$ is connected to another function $g$ if their difference $g - f$ takes on a value of at most $d$ in at least $i$ positions, is called the $d$-Hamming graph. It can be shown that for any given function $h$, there exists a unique eigenvector $v$ in the $d$-Hamming graph, where the support of $v$ has minimal size, and this can be used to establish exact bounds on the size of the largest eigenvalue. These bounds can further be applied to determine the minimum amount of information needed to reliably communicate data from a set of sensors to a central hub over a channel with noise.

COPASI is a widely-used biochemical network simulation and analysis software with a extensive feature set, but its standalone application lacks interactivity. To address this, the ShinyCOPASI web interface was developed for interactive modeling and analysis within a web browser, offering many of the original toolset's capabilities. To further enhance interaction with COPASI models, the ShinyCOPASI server allows users to upload local models into the online platform, providing multiple model comparison capabilities. In addition, the interface has been optimized for data visualization and exporting results. Here, the ShinyCOPASI server's functionality and usage are detailed, along with a step-by-step guide for users to access and interact with available models.

This study reveals the limitations of neural networks when used to solve inverse problems, highlighting their inability to provide accurate solutions for a range of problem instances. Conversely, neural networks can be adapted to tackle ill-posed problems, as they can develop unique solutions by imposing regulatory constraints. By employing differential equations as regularizers in inverse problems, the proposed method leverages a problem-specific neural network to enhance an initial solution and achieve improved results. Experimentally, our study demonstrates the superiority of our solution in both diffusion and tomography inverse problems.
We identify the domain of definition for the $*$-representation of $SU_q(2)$, and its class function algebra being a MASA (maximal abelian self-adjoint algebra) provided that $|q| < 1$.

For large multi-agent reinforcement learning problems, a key challenge lies in generating a good reinforcement policy relatively quickly. In this context, policy iteration, which involves taking the maximum over all possible policies, becomes too computationally expensive, even with a 10,000-state environment, where it's roughly 25% faster than other methods but still too slow. We'll show that, by approximating the policy iteration step, specifically by accepting an inexact gradient, a significantly faster yet convergent iterative process can be achieved, where this approach is 5-10% faster. This new method shares similarities with inexact Newton's method from optimization and shares a similar rate of convergence, both in theory and in practice. We'll also demonstrate that the computational expense of each iteration is relatively constant, whereas traditional policy iteration experiences increasing costs as it progresses. We'll examine the efficacy of this approach on large MDPs with up to 10,000 states and 100 actions and find it outperforms other methods, where inexact GMRES policy iteration outperforms even the faster iterative methods by 5-10%. We'll also provide a theoretical framework for selecting the parameters in inexact GMRES policy iteration. In a large MDP setting, with 10,000 states and 100 actions, inexact GMRES policy iteration converges at a rate comparable to that of model-free Q-learning, yet outperforms it, where inexact GMRES policy iteration outperforms the other methods by

Edge ideals associated with weighted oriented graphs, concerning edges and weights, have previously been studied for unweighted graphs. A new class, called weighted oriented graphs, is now being investigated, which includes oriented graphs as a special case. The edge ideal of a weighted oriented graph, represented by $I(G)$, is defined based on its edges and weights. For certain weighted oriented graphs, it has been demonstrated that $I^2_G = I^{\neq 2}_G$ and that the number of minimal generators of $I_G$ corresponds to the binomial dimension of $k[G]$. Furthermore, the proposed method can resolve the binomial nature of an edge ideal given a finite set of elements in a polynomial ring.

This study proposes a novel and streamlined approach for evaluating a computational model in scenarios where input-output relationships are reversed. Typically, inverse problems are challenging because they often rely on imperfect or incomplete data and demand a comprehensive exploration of possible solutions. To overcome these issues, the proposed method utilizes a modified version of an existing probabilistic algorithm designed to generate likely solutions based on the model's confidence in predicted outcomes. To test its effectiveness, the study conducts a pilot investigation involving a simple educational model of a basic control system and a specific goal in an online game known as 'Dodge This'. The goal involves guiding a player character to avoid collision with an oncoming obstacle. Due to the model's simplicity, the study searches for the closest possible solution to the target outcome using a comprehensive search algorithm and compares it with the proposed method's results. The latter uses the generated probability distribution to identify the most suitable solution, which converges with the exact solution as the number of iterations increases. The resulting output shows that the proposed method yields solutions closer to the exact solution than those produced by standard probabilistic algorithms, especially for shorter simulation runs, although it takes longer to reach the exact solution outcome.

This research investigates the relationship between concept class size and data distribution complexity, providing a precise bound on how well these factors influence robustness in the learning process. Specifically, it considers the impact of partial coverage on robustness and demonstrates that, above a certain radius, some concept classes are not robustly learnable in a given data distribution. To overcome this limitation, it proposes a data preprocessing technique, involving radius adjustment, to facilitate distribution-free robust learning. This technique is demonstrated on $k$-center clustering and shown to be effective in multiple clustering algorithms, such as $k$-center clustering, slope-one clustering, and Trimethylamine clustering. Furthermore, it examines the statistical properties of distribution-free learning and identifies criteria for when robust learning is possible. This research explores the influence of data distribution on robust learning and highlights the distinction between finite and infinite data sets. Finally, it investigates the connection between robustness and data distribution and challenges the assumption that robustness is solely determined by data coverage. Instead, it proposes that concentration phenomena, like subgaussian phenomena, play a crucial role in robust learning.

This study uses theoretical models to examine how a lone photon affects the formation of quark and gluon pairs, and the motion of an existing photon when present in a proton-proton collision. Researchers looked at how this photon, embedded in one of the protons, influences the creation of a second jet when compared to events producing only one jet. Their analysis considered both central and off-axis collisions at various energy levels, specifically at 13 TeV, and accounted for different stability criteria. It was observed that including the photon's influence on initial conditions makes the parton's momentum less stable, but chooses values closer to its original location, resulting in parton pairs being chosen over more massive configurations. This choice introduces a bias, affecting the jet's momentum when it reaches the stable configuration. To quantify this effect, researchers calculated the rapidity distribution, and the difference between being a quark or gluon on one of the jets. Their results showed a 4% probability for the photon to be part of the quark, and a 20% likelihood for it to be part of the gluon, and predicted a 0.56% deviation between these two scenarios for the differential cross section at 13 TeV.

This study examines whether certain specialized mathematical values, known as multiple zeta values (MZVs), can be obtained by combining simpler values, specifically reduced MZVs, to a lesser degree in alternating versions of certain complex mathematical series, specifically those involving factorial components. The investigation demonstrates that alternating versions of these series, called alternating Apéry series, can be represented by combining MZVs special values at a lower level of complexity, specifically the fourth level, as opposed to their non-alternating counterparts which require a higher level, specifically the sixth. The proof relies on a recently proposed relationship between MZVs and their reduced counterparts, as well as their connection to more complex mathematical series, specifically those involving factorial components, called super-differential relations.

We have discovered a new brown dwarf, which we are designating SDWD01, in the constellation of Capricornus. Utilizing trigonometric parallactic deviation, we measured the object's distance and velocity. The measurement of its proper motion revealed a significant value of 246.38 mas/year. Over the past 90 years, there has been a notable change in its position, indicating a velocity of approximately 21.6 km/s. Its estimated distance is roughly 125.5 parsecs, and we consider it to be a low-mass object with a mass of around 15 to 20 Jupiter masses, based on its location in the color-magnitude diagram. It is most likely a remote rogue brown dwarf in our galaxy, and its low luminosity makes it challenging to detect objects at similar ages and distances.

Our study examines the production of particles such as p, $\pi$, K, and p in collisions at the CERN LHC's ALICE detector, exploring a comprehensive range of centralities from 0 to 80\% and collision energies of 2.76 and 5.02 TeV. The analysis focuses on comparing and understanding proton-$\pi$ and proton/K ratios across various collision energies and system sizes, either by fixing the collision energy or the system size. Observations indicate that while the ratios exhibit expected increase with decreasing system size, characteristic of parton spin effects, they also display an energy-dependent trend, with the influence of parton spin increasing by about 20\% as the energy rises from 2.76 to 5.02 TeV. This is particularly evident when examining the smallest collision systems and tends to be more pronounced for strange particles. The data are compared to the EPOS LHC simulation model and theoretical explanations are proposed to account for these phenomena.

A long-standing challenge in high-energy physics has been to formally derive double parton distribution functions (DPDs) and understand their relationship with single parton distribution functions (PDFs). Despite previous claims of resolution, the issue remains contentious. In our analysis, we argue that DPDs cannot be linked to PDFs in a manifestly renormalizable theory. This conclusion arises from examining College on Mass Spectrometry a manifestly renormalizable triparton distribution and observing collinear and transverseness properties. The findings suggest that DPDs are inherently noncollinear and cannot be connected to PDFs as previously proposed.

Two major asteroids provide essential materials, specifically basalts, dolerites, and other rock types, via two primary means: first, by delivering these materials to other planets and moons; second, by making available the remnants of these materials from impact events. The Martian and Lunar regolith materials, resulting from such events, hold great potential for use in extraterrestrial construction and manufacturing due to their accessibility. To facilitate accurate predictions regarding the availability and quality of these materials for future missions, TLAR's Lunar Resource Map has been developed. This innovative tool generates maps indicating the presence, quality, and predicted thickness of regolith materials across the Moon's surface. The method employs impact crater data and statistical analysis to determine these factors. The maps are created using a simple, user-friendly interface that allows for visualizations, including the maps themselves, and associated statistics, such as the total amount of regolith material, its median thickness, and the quality across specific regions of the Moon's surface. The maps are further customizable, enabling users to adjust the quality metrics to match their specific needs. The visualizations and associated data are made publicly accessible via a website, designed for ease of use, including interactive 3D models of the Moon's surface, which provide a clearer understanding of the regolith materials and their distribution. The site also offers tools for downloading the data in multiple formats, such as KML and CSV. The Lunar Resource Map tool is set to analyze the Martian regolith materials in the future.

When a liquid film surrounds a fibre, experiencing a slip condition due to
wall friction, the points where the slip occurs can cause the liquid to form distinct drops. This process is facilitated through a numerical model that accounts for the fibre's internal structure, presenting a novel approach in this field. As a result, the method can be used in various scenarios to predict how a liquid reacts to slip at the molecular level, leading to physically accurate simulations. This is particularly important as the resulting drop formation significantly affects the fibre's wetting characteristics. To verify the model's accuracy, researchers compared it with existing experiments and non-linear calculations, finding a strong connection. This verification further enabled the analysis of how the liquid surrounds the fibre, especially when the slip condition changes, resulting in the creation of far-reaching liquid filaments and complex drop patterns. This complex behaviour was thoroughly investigated, providing new insights into drop formation and filament creation. This study has implications in understanding wetting and sticking mechanisms, especially when these processes occur on a microscopic scale, which is crucial in industrial applications such as card printing and fibre treatment.

We utilize data from 34 spiral galaxies with directly measured star formation rates to evaluate the reliability of stellar population inference in the Prospector framework. Our study reveals that the current implementation underestimates star formation rates by approximately 0.1 dex and demonstrates how increasing the Br$\gamma$ luminosity evolution category can mitigate these errors. Furthermore, although Prospector accurately models the broad distribution of galaxy spectra, biases in star formation rate predictions are not significantly mitigated. To address this, we suggest refining the model by incorporating a more detailed grid of star formation rate templates and utilizing stellar mass observations to constrain stellar population history. Additionally, we note that Prospector's uncertainty quantification somewhat compensates for the biases in a median sense. Our findings are anticipated to enhance the accuracy of stellar population inference in the Prospector pipeline and guide future development.

We introduce a concept of quadratic categories, representing a higher-dimensional extension of 2-CY categories with predefined orbifolds, and show that these categories have an inherent hierarchy of braided auto-equivalences.  It's observed that these categories have a natural relationship with the full duals of higher-dimensional mirror theory and exceptional braided auto-equivalences of orbifolds.  Moreover, we find that the exceptional braided auto-equivalences of some specific types of orbifolds can be mapped one-to-one to certain types of quadratic categories.  This mapping allows us to derive the formula for the second mutation of a quiver and establishes a connection between the value of $\mathfrak{e}$ in the Caucher-Kovalevskaya extension and the Frobenius-Albert structure, allowing us to calculate its value for any quadratic category.  This value, it's noted, is equivalent to the number of points in the maximal torus of the exceptional orbifold it represents.  This exceptional value is found to be 296, and we propose that this is the smallest possible value for any exceptional braided auto-equivalence.  We also find that the exceptional orbifold with this minimal value is homotopy equivalent to the space of isometries of a 14-dimensional lattice, and that its A-D dual is the 15-dimensional lattice itself.  This provides a way to resolve the ambiguity in the numerical value of the structural invariant of the Caucher-K

Our primary objective is to demonstrate that the Fisher-KPP equation has a smooth solution given an initial condition with certain regularity properties. Specifically, we'll show that if the initial condition has a specific higher differentiability and is bounded in a particular space, the solution will also have those same properties for all subsequent time points. Ultimately, we'll prove that the solution is infinitely differentiable in space and temporally, provided the initial condition is similarly smooth.
